question: Why do people in Victorian photographs so rarely smile, even once exposures had dropped to a second or two?
answer: Convention. Portrait photographs followed painting, where a broad open smile belonged to drunks, fools and peasants in comic scenes; dignity meant a closed mouth. Smiling for the camera spread in the twentieth century with cheap snapshot cameras and advertising full of happy families. The stiff Victorian face was a choice about how to be remembered.
move: When everyone does the same odd thing, look for the rule behind it.
ask: Which of my habits is only a convention I have never questioned?
source: Kotchemidova, Critical Studies in Media Communication, 2005
reference: Christina Kotchemidova, Why we say cheese: producing the smile in snapshot photography, Critical Studies in Media Communication, 2005
